latin.219: GAR. Resp. Minorem non esse simpliciter veram, si audiatur Camero praelect. de verbo Dei cap. 7. Summum hominis bonum est animi & corporis, adeoque totius hominis status perfectus atque omnibus numeris absolutus, nihil ut ultra requiri vel debeat, vel possit amplius. Hic vero status & conditio est imago Dei. Ceterum imago Dei in duobus sita est, in sanctitate, & qua sanctitatem sequitur, beata immortalitate. Si vita promissa Adae erat status ipsius perfectus, & ea vita consistit in sanctitate. Ergo vita promissa consistebat in sanctitate. Nec aliter Clar. Amyraldus, De trib. foeder. Thes. II. Promissio foederis illius primi consistere debuit in vita perpetua, & affluente omni bonorum genere, qua tum in animum, tum in corpus hominis competere potuissent. Justitia autem & sanctitas nonne inter animi bona censeri debent?
latin.220: PLAC. Quis non videt a praestantissimo Camerone describi eo loco, non vitam quatenus promissa Adamo sub perfectae obedientiae conditione fuerat, sed absolute summum hominis bonum, quale Dei verbo seu Euangelio promittitur? Differt autem admodum id quod foedere gratiae promittitur, ab eo quod foedere naturae promittebatur Adamo. Quis etiam non videt, Clariss. Collegam D. Amyraldum bona intelligere, ut ita loquar, physica, non autem ea quae mere moralia erant, quorumque continuatio exigebatur ab Adamo?
latin.221: Itaque inseruerat haec verba, in statu integrae naturae constituti, & subiunxerat ista eaque in paradiso Terrestri fruenda, quae cur sint a Viro Docto omissa, aliis judicandum relinquo. Innuunt certe supponi integritatis moralis Naturae conservationem, promitti reliquorum omnium bonorum in paradiso Terrestri fruendorum continuationem. Nam, ut Minorem negatam probem, si comminabatur Deus Adamo tanquam poenam, amissionem seu privationem justitiae originalis, certe pollicebatur tanquam praemium, non-amissionem seu conservationem justitiae originalis, quomodo igitur fieri potuit ut eam Adamus amitteret? Pollicebatur, inquies, sub conditione. Quanam? si perseveraret in integritate & justitia? Si permaneret in obedientia erga Deum? Si non peccaret? Quocunque nomine eam voces, idem erit cum re promissa, & conditio promissionis cum re promissa confundetur.
latin.222: GAR. Hoc iterum inficiamur. Quia justitia & sanctitas Adami duplex constitui potest. Altera naturalis, altera supernaturalis: altera viae, altera patriae; altera hominis creati, altera hominis glorificati. Justitia naturalis & hominis creati quae justitia viae dici potest, erat conditio promissionis; sed supernaturalis, & hominis glorificati, quam dicimus justitiam patriae, erat res promissa.
latin.223: PLAC. Hac responsione sibi Vir Doctus aperte contradicit, & cum videatur respondere, non respondet tamen, sed dat manus. Agebatur enim de justitia originali, ut patet ex meo argumento. Utra igitur duarum illarum, quas distinxit, justitiarum est justitia originalis? Num illa supernaturalis, patriae, hominis glorificati? Non certe. Non enim illa Adamus priusquam peccaret praeditus erat: non illam erat propagaturus in posteros. Est igitur justitia naturalis, viae, hominis creati, justitia originalis de qua agebatur in argumento? Atqui Vir doctus confitetur hanc Justitiam fuisse conditionem promissionis. Confitetur ergo non fuisse promissam: id quod probare institueram, & ipse negaverat. Quod si non fuit promissa, eius privatio non fuit mors comminatione denunciata. Id quod mihi probandum incumbebat.
latin.224: Ceterum libenter quaesiverim, unde habuerit Vir Doctus foedere naturae, cuius conditio fuit justitia naturalis, promissam fuisse justitiam supernaturalem? Id ne alicubi dicit Scriptura? An potest ratiocinando ex Naturae contemplatione colligi? Quaero etiam unde habuerit, Adami, qui e terra fuit, terrenus, & cuius paradisus fuit in terra, patriam non fuisse terram? Tollere certe videtur discrimen inter foedus naturae & foedus gratiae, primum hominem & secundum, & aliquid docere, immo Dei voluntatem quandam & promissionem confingere praeter Scripturam. Id quod omni Christiano, praecipue inter Reformatos Theologiae professori summa cura vitandum est.

pass_a.219: GAR. Reply. That the minor is not simply true, if Cameron is heard, lecture on the word of God chapter 7. The highest good of man is of soul and body, and so the perfect state of the whole man and absolute in every respect, so that nothing further ought to be required, or can be any more. But this state and condition is the image of God. Moreover the image of God is seated in two things, in sanctity, and in the blessed immortality which follows sanctity. If the life promised to Adam was his perfect state, and that life consists in sanctity. Therefore the promised life consisted in sanctity. And not otherwise the most illustrious Amyraut, On the three covenants, Thesis II. The promise of that first covenant ought to have consisted in perpetual life, and abounding with every kind of goods which could have belonged then to the mind, then to the body of man. But ought not justice and sanctity to be counted among the goods of the mind?
pass_a.220: PLAC. Who does not see that by the most excellent Cameron there is described in that place, not life insofar as it had been promised to Adam under the condition of perfect obedience, but absolutely the highest good of man, such as is promised by the word of God or the Gospel? But what is promised by the covenant of grace differs greatly from what was being promised to Adam by the covenant of nature. Who also does not see that the most illustrious colleague D. Amyraut understands goods, so to speak, physical, not however those which were merely moral, and whose continuation was being required from Adam?
pass_a.221: And so he had inserted these words, constituted in the state of integral nature, and had subjoined those things also to be enjoyed in the earthly paradise, which why they were omitted by the learned man, I leave to others to judge. They certainly hint that the conservation of the moral integrity of Nature is presupposed, that the continuation of all the remaining goods to be enjoyed in the earthly paradise is promised. For, that I may prove the denied Minor, if God was threatening Adam as a penalty with the loss or privation of original justice, certainly he was promising as a reward the non-loss or conservation of original justice; how then could it happen that Adam should lose it? He was promising, you will say, under a condition. Which? if he persevered in integrity and justice? If he remained in obedience toward God? If he did not sin? By whatever name you call it, it will be the same as the thing promised, and the condition of the promise will be confused with the thing promised.
pass_a.222: GAR. This again we deny. Because the justice and sanctity of Adam can be constituted as twofold. One natural, the other supernatural: one of the way, the other of the homeland; one of created man, the other of glorified man. The natural justice and of created man which can be called justice of the way was the condition of the promise; but the supernatural, and of glorified man, which we call justice of the homeland, was the thing promised.
pass_a.223: PLAC. By this reply the learned man openly contradicts himself, and while he seems to reply, he does not reply nevertheless, but gives his hands. For the matter was about original justice, as is clear from my argument. Which then of those two justices which he distinguished is original justice? Is it that supernatural one, of the homeland, of glorified man? Certainly not. For Adam was not endowed with that before he sinned: he was not going to propagate that into posterity. Is it therefore the natural justice, of the way, of created man, the original justice about which the argument was concerned? But the learned man confesses that this Justice was the condition of the promise. He confesses therefore that it was not promised: which is what I had set out to prove, and he himself had denied. But if it was not promised, its privation was not the death denounced by the threat. Which is what it was incumbent on me to prove.
pass_a.224: For the rest I would gladly inquire whence the learned man had it that by the covenant of nature, whose condition was natural justice, supernatural justice had been promised? Does Scripture say that anywhere? Or can it be gathered by reasoning from contemplation of Nature? I ask also whence he had it that Adam, who was from the earth, earthly, and whose paradise was on earth, did not have the earth as homeland? He certainly seems to remove the distinction between the covenant of nature and the covenant of grace, the first man and the second, and to teach something, indeed to invent a certain will and promise of God beyond Scripture. Which every Christian, especially a professor of Theology among the Reformed, must avoid with utmost care.

219: GAR. Reply. The minor is not simply true, if one hears Cameron, Lectures on the Word of God, chapter 7: "Man's highest good is a perfect state of soul and body—of the whole man—complete in every respect, so that nothing further can or ought to be asked. This state and condition is the image of God. The image of God sits in two things: sanctity, and the blessed immortality that follows sanctity." If the life promised to Adam was his perfect state, and that life consists in sanctity, then the promised life consisted in sanctity.

Nor does the most illustrious Amyraut speak otherwise, On the Three Covenants, Thesis II: "The promise of that first covenant had to consist in perpetual life, abounding in every kind of good that could belong to man's mind and body." But ought not justice and sanctity to be counted among the goods of the mind?
220: PLAC. Who does not see that the most excellent Cameron is describing there not the life promised to Adam under the condition of perfect obedience, but absolutely man's highest good as the Word of God—or the Gospel—promises it? What the covenant of grace promises differs sharply from what the covenant of nature was promising Adam.
Who also does not see that our most illustrious colleague Amyraut means, so to speak, physical goods—not the merely moral ones whose continuance God was requiring of Adam?
221: So Amyraut had inserted the words "constituted in the state of integral nature," and had added "and those things to be enjoyed in the earthly paradise"—why the learned man omitted them I leave others to judge. They clearly presuppose conservation of nature's moral integrity and promise continuance of the remaining goods to be enjoyed in the earthly paradise.

To prove the denied minor: if God threatened Adam, as penalty, with loss or privation of original justice, then as reward He was promising non-loss—conservation—of that justice. How then could Adam lose it? "He promised under a condition," you say. Which? If he persevered in integrity and justice? Remained obedient to God? Did not sin? Call it what you will: it is the same as the thing promised, and the condition of the promise is confused with the thing promised.
222: GAR. We deny this again. Adam's justice and sanctity admit a twofold account: natural versus supernatural; of the way versus of the homeland; of created man versus of glorified man.
Natural justice—created man's justice of the way—was only the condition of the promise. Supernatural justice—glorified man's justice of the homeland—was the thing promised.
223: PLAC. This answer openly contradicts the learned man himself. He seems to reply, yet does not—he yields. We were arguing about original justice, as my case shows. Of the two justices he split apart, which is original? The supernatural homeland justice of glorified man? No. Adam lacked that before the fall and was never going to hand it down.

So original justice in the argument is natural justice—of the way, of created man. But Garissoles admits that justice was the condition of the promise. He therefore admits it was not promised—the very point I meant to prove, which he had denied. If it was not promised, losing it was not the death the threat denounced. That is what I had to establish.
224: Beyond that I would gladly know Garissoles' source for saying the covenant of nature—conditioned on natural justice—promised supernatural justice. Where does Scripture say so? Can bare contemplation of nature prove it by reasoning?

And where did he get the claim that Adam—earthly, from the earth, with an earthly paradise—did not have earth for his homeland? That erases the line between nature's covenant and grace's, between the first man and the second, and invents a divine will and promise beyond Scripture. No Christian—least of all a Reformed professor of theology—may risk that.
